analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 50 or more workers to offer affordable family health coverage and pay a set share of the premium.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Labor Committee from April 1998 until that Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a new title to the Fair Labor Standards Act requiring every employer with at least 50 workers to offer a family health plan at least as good as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan offered to federal employees, and to pay a share of the premium at least equal to what the federal government pays for federal workers. Coverage would have had to begin within 30 days of hiring, contract workers would count as employees, and the Labor Department could fine employers who did not comply. The bill never moved after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Working families — including part-time workers and contract workers — at large employers who today lack health coverage or lack coverage for their spouses and children. The bill's own findings cite roughly 41 million uninsured Americans, most of them workers or their dependents. Workers already on Medicare, Medicaid, or military family coverage could shift to the employer plan, with the federal program covering the employee's premium share if they asked.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each large employer to offer every employee the chance to enroll in a qualifying plan covering the employee and family, with the employer paying at least the same premium share the federal government pays for the FEHBP Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard Plan [S2] [S3].
Coverage would have to begin within 30 days of an employee's first hour of work, and contract workers would be treated as employees, closing a common gap in employer coverage [S3] [S2].
Part-time workers under 30 hours get a prorated employer contribution, and workers under 10 hours get no required contribution but keep access to the offer [S3] [S2].
The Labor Department could bring civil actions, assess civil money penalties, and seek injunctions against employers that fail to comply, giving the mandate real enforcement teeth [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 50 or more employees bear a new premium contribution requirement; employees who enroll pay the remaining share through payroll withholding; and federal programs — Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, and CHAMPUS — would pay the employee share of premiums for enrollees who request it, moving some costs onto those programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers and federal health programs

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate is a new payroll cost on firms with 50 or more employees, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that such costs can show up as slower hiring, lower wages, or pressure to keep headcount under the threshold [S3].

The bill requires employees covered by Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, or CHAMPUS to accept the employer offer or have the federal program pay the employee premium share, which shifts costs onto those programs and can move people out of public coverage into employer plans they did not choose [S3] [S2].
Employers pay nothing for employees working fewer than 10 hours a week, leaving the shortest-hours workers — disproportionately low-wage — without a guaranteed employer contribution [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered guaranteed family coverage to a large share of the uninsured workforce at the price of a mandatory employer contribution, with the premium benchmark tied to a plan federal workers already receive so benefits were concrete and defined. The main honest objection is the burden on mid-sized employers and the risk that mandate costs are partly passed back to workers, and the design pushes some federal-program enrollees onto employer plans. On balance it was a substantial, enforceable coverage expansion, but it was never examined in committee, so its cost estimates and side effects were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Kennedy introduced the bill on April 22, 1998, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S1] [S5] [S3].
No cosponsors signed on [S4], and the bill's only further activity was a second set of introductory remarks by the sponsor in September 1998 [S5].
The bill stayed in committee until the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, with no committee or floor action recorded [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers never faced the coverage mandate, and the health insurance status quo continued with tens of millions uninsured. No member besides the sponsor ever had to take a position on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large employers and the uninsured status quo

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks on the floor in April and again in September 1998, and referred it to the Labor Committee where he could not schedule action himself.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. James Jeffords (R-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in April 1998 and never held a hearing or markup; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: The 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: No member cosponsored the bill and no other senator brought it to the floor; the employer-mandate approach drew no bipartisan support that session.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape is unknown; the record shows a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and a bill referred to a committee that never acted [S4] [S5].

industries.note: They would owe a mandatory premium contribution for every employee and family, with civil fines and injunctions for noncompliance, and contract workers would count toward the mandate. Their interest in avoiding the cost runs directly against workers' interest in getting covered.

The mandate would have created millions of new premium-paying customers routed through employer-sponsored private insurance, with issuers required to certify that their group plans meet the federal benchmark. Workers would gain coverage, but through private insurers made the permanent channel for it.

industries.industry: Federal health programs (Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, CHAMPUS)
industries.note: Enrollees could demand that the federal program pay the employee share of employer-plan premiums, shifting federal spending toward private employer coverage. Some cost would move off the uninsured rolls and onto program budgets.
